title: Decoda & Fullscript: Integrated Supplements 2026
summary: With Decoda Health's Fullscript integration, supplement protocols follow the clinical note automatically. No tab switching required.
body_markdown:
## What Fullscript Is and Why It Matters for Elective Care


Fullscript is a practitioner-led supplement dispensing and care planning tool used by[125,000+ providers and 10M+ patients cumulatively](https://fullscript.com/en-US/qualitycare) across North America. Providers recommend professional-grade supplements and lab tests directly through it, and patients order online with products shipped to their door.


For elective care practices (med spas, wellness clinics, longevity practices), this matters because supplements are increasingly part of the service mix. Weight management protocols, hormone optimization, skin health, and recovery programs all commonly include a nutritional component. Without a structured dispensing tool, recommendations often get lost between the appointment and the front door. Fullscript keeps that recommendation in the clinical record, gives patients a simple way to follow through, and routes a share of the revenue back to the practice. The Decoda Health and Fullscript partnership is what brings that dispensing into the chart itself.


## How Supplement Dispensing Fits Into an Elective Care Practice


Supplement dispensing used to live almost exclusively in functional medicine and naturopathic offices. That has shifted. Wellness clinics, longevity practices,[medical spas](https://decodahealth.com/blog/top-medspa-ehr-software) , and hybrid aesthetics practices are all building nutritional protocols into their care plans because patients are asking for them and the clinical case is straightforward.


Patients are already buying supplements — the global dietary supplements market was[valued at $209.5 billion in 2025](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/dietary-supplements-market-report) and is projected to reach $414.5 billion by 2033 at an 8.9% CAGR. The question for a practice is not whether patients take supplements. It is whether they take the ones you would have chosen, bought somewhere you had no visibility into. Someone coming in for a[GLP-1 weight loss program](https://decodahealth.com/blog/glp-1-programs-compounding-pharmacy-integration) or a hormone optimization consult increasingly expects a recommendation as part of the visit, and will fill the gap from a retail shelf if you don't give them one.


For practice owners that raises a second question: how do you make that recommendation without adding another manual step to an already stretched clinical workflow? A protocol written on a notepad rarely turns into a purchase. One built inside the[clinical charting record](https://decodahealth.com/products/notes) does.


## What a Fullscript EHR Integration Actually Does


The Decoda Health and Fullscript partnership makes this concrete. At the most basic level, a dispensing provider's Fullscript practitioner account is connected once from inside Decoda Health. After that, providers can pull up a patient chart, select products from the Fullscript catalog, and send a supplement plan directly to the patient without opening a second tab.


The patient receives a link, orders from home, and the product ships to their door — with the recommendation logged against the visit that produced it.


The functional case for this is clear. According to Fullscript, practices see a[16% monthly revenue increase after integrating](https://fullscript.com/blog/charm-and-fullscript-integration) and write 33% more supplement recommendations per week. The gap between "I recommend this" and "the patient actually buys it" closes when ordering takes one step instead of five.


## How Supplement Plans Connect to Patient Adherence


Writing a plan is the easy part. Getting patients to follow it is something else, and that gap is where the integration earns its keep.


Fullscript's own adherence data points at the refill, not the recommendation: patients on auto-refill are[70% more likely to order their next product](https://fullscript.com/adherence-insights) . That is the part of the protocol a practice can actually influence from inside the chart, because it depends on the plan being set up correctly at the visit rather than on the patient remembering to reorder eight weeks later.


On the patient side, Fullscript's mobile app includes dose reminders, refill prompts, and product context embedded directly in the plan. Patients can see what they ordered, when to take it, and why, removing the friction of a recommendation with no follow-through pathway.


## Supplement Protocols Within a Broader Care Plan


Supplement protocols work best when they follow the clinical logic of the visit. A provider reviewing lab results and documenting a clinical note who closes the chart without connecting those findings to a nutritional recommendation is leaving part of the care plan unwritten.


The cleaner model treats the supplement plan as a structured output of the clinical visit. After a hormone panel, the provider recommends targeted support. After a GLP-1 intake visit, they build a[longevity medicine protocol](https://decodahealth.com/blog/add-longevity-services-med-spa) around muscle preservation and micronutrient repletion. The supplement plan follows the clinical reasoning, lives in the same record, and gets updated as[multi-year longevity protocols](https://decodahealth.com/who-we-serve/longevity) shift or treatment phases change.


This also shapes how patients experience continuity of care. A[patient treatment plan](https://decodahealth.com/products/care-plans) that evolves alongside their chart feels like ongoing clinical guidance. A one-time emailed PDF from six months ago does not.


## Fullscript's Quality Standards for Professional-Grade Supplements


Recommending a supplement is a clinical act. Whatever goes on that plan reflects on the provider who signed off on it, which is why the source of those products matters — and why the vetting behind the catalog is worth understanding before you dispense from it.


Fullscript runs a[published quality program](https://fullscript.com/quality-program) that goes beyond a one-time sign-up checklist. Every brand is vetted by its clinical team before a product reaches the catalog, product labelling and claims are verified, and its QA team reviews brand site licences annually rather than only at onboarding.


The catalog includes brands practitioners in elective care already recognize: Thorne, Pure Encapsulations, Nordic Naturals, Metagenics, Integrative Therapeutics, and 300-plus others. These are professional-grade lines that typically require a practitioner account to access, so patients cannot simply pick them up at a pharmacy.


For practice owners, this distinction carries real weight. A product that turns out to be mislabeled or underdosed is a credibility problem, and in some cases a liability one. Fullscript's quality standards give practices a defensible answer to the question of why they recommend what they recommend.


## What a Practice Actually Earns on Fullscript Dispensing


This is the part most write-ups skip, and it is the part that decides whether dispensing is worth the setup.


The first thing to know is that the default earns you nothing. New Fullscript accounts open as[no-profit dispensaries](https://support.fullscript.com/articles/profit-dispensaries) : patients get 10% off every order and the practice takes 0% margin. Converting to a profit account is a deliberate step that requires direct deposit details and tax information, which is why practices that connect Fullscript and never revisit the settings can dispense for months without earning on a single order.


Once converted, you set the patient discount, and that number is the margin dial. The US ceiling is 35%, and the discount and your margin come out of the same 35 points — extend the maximum discount to patients and you earn 0% on those orders. Most practices land somewhere in the middle, treating a modest patient discount as the reason the patient orders through you instead of a marketplace. Earnings accrue as orders ship and pay out to your bank account every 30 days.


Multi-provider clinics have one more decision, and it maps onto how you already pay people. Fullscript can compensate on a *patient owner* basis, where a provider earns on everything their assigned patients buy, or a *plan author* basis, where a provider earns only on what they personally recommended. The second matches how most elective care practices think about provider production; the first is simpler to administer. Pick one before you turn dispensing on, because reassigning attribution after the fact is manual work.


## Why Integration Matters More Than a Separate Storefront


Most practices weighing this are not choosing between a standalone Fullscript account and an integrated one. They are choosing between three things, and the storefront question is the last of them.


**Carrying physical stock.** The traditional answer, and the expensive one. Retail supplements tie up cash in inventory, take shelf space, require someone to count and reorder them, and expire on your balance sheet rather than the manufacturer's. A direct-to-patient dispensary removes all of that: your clinic counts no bottles, carries no shelf, and writes off no expired stock, while still capturing the margin.


**Not dispensing at all.** Also a real choice, and the one that quietly loses. The patient still takes supplements — she buys them from a retail shelf or a marketplace listing, at a quality tier you did not choose, in doses you did not set, with no record of it in her chart when she reports a reaction six weeks later.


**A standalone account, outside the chart.** This works, and it is where most practices start. The problem is what happens in between: the provider has to remember to switch tabs, pull up the right patient, and build the plan before the next appointment starts. Some do. Many don't, especially on busy days — and a recommendation that never gets sent is a protocol that never gets followed, plus a clinical record that doesn't reflect what the provider actually advised.


Integration closes that last gap. The plan gets built inside the same workflow as the clinical note, linked to the same patient, visible to the same team.


## What Practices Should Confirm Before Connecting Fullscript to Their EMR


Before connecting Fullscript to any EMR, a few things are worth confirming upfront.


Area to Confirm


What to Know Before Going Live


Provider accounts


Each dispensing practitioner typically needs their own Fullscript account connected individually. In multi-provider practices, setup multiplies by the number of prescribing providers.


Account type & margin


New accounts open as no-profit dispensaries — patients get 10% off and the practice earns 0%. Converting requires direct deposit and tax details. The US patient discount ceiling is 35%, and discount and margin come out of the same 35 points.


Data sync scope


The recommendation is sent and logged in the clinical record, but product details do not auto-populate structured chart fields. The plan lives in Fullscript; the chart reflects that a plan was sent, with no full bidirectional sync.


Role-based permissions


For[multi-location practices](https://decodahealth.com/blog/weight-loss-practice-software-that-scales) with role-based access, verify whether the EMR restricts which staff roles can initiate a recommendation. Some configurations allow front desk staff to view plans but not create them.


Native vs. third-party connection


Confirm the EMR's Fullscript connection is native and production-ready. A native integration means patient matching happens automatically inside the chart workflow; third-party workarounds require manual steps.


Going in with accurate expectations prevents retrofitting the workflow after the first busy week.

Once connected within Decoda Health, supplement plans become a structured output of the clinical visit — and the revenue they generate reports alongside the visits, memberships, and packages already on the patient's record, rather than in a separate dashboard nobody opens.


## Final Thoughts on the Decoda Health and Fullscript Partnership


Dispensing is worth doing when the protocol is part of the visit and the margin is set deliberately rather than left on the default. Get those two right and supplements stop being a side conversation at checkout — they become a documented part of the care plan that patients actually follow, and a revenue line you can see.[Schedule a short intro call](https://calendly.com/d/cr5z-78z-8zq/decoda-ai-intro) to see the Decoda Health and Fullscript partnership in action.

Yes. For hybrid practices running surgical and wellness services under one roof, this means the provider moves from a post-op note to a lab order to a supplement protocol inside a single workflow, with every action logged to the same patient record.

Once a practitioner's Fullscript account is connected within Decoda Health, supplement plans are built and sent from inside the chart — no second login, no manual patient matching, no tab switching. The provider finishes a visit, Decoda Health's AI Scribe drafts the clinical note, and the supplement protocol goes to the patient from the same workflow. The recommendation is tied to the visit record automatically, so the clinical reasoning and the nutritional plan stay in the same place.

Fullscript reports that patients on auto-refill are 70% more likely to order their next product, which is the clearest adherence signal it publishes. Treat it as a workflow instruction rather than a forecast: the refill setting is chosen when the plan is built, so the plans that hold up are the ones finished during the visit rather than after it. Patients also receive dose reminders, refill prompts, and product context directly in the Fullscript mobile app, which removes the follow-through gap that typically opens between a verbal recommendation and a purchase.

A standalone Fullscript account works, but the recommendation gap is real. When Fullscript lives outside the clinical record, the provider has to remember to switch tabs, find the right patient, build the plan, and send it before the next appointment — steps that get skipped on busy days. The recommendation never gets sent, the protocol never gets followed, and the clinical record does not reflect what the provider actually intended. Integration ties the supplement plan to the visit that generated it, so the recommendation is a structured output of the appointment rather than a separate task that competes with the rest of the schedule.

The recommendation stays logged in the clinical record regardless of whether the follow-up happens. Patients retain access to their plan through the Fullscript mobile app, which includes dose reminders and refill prompts, so the protocol continues even when the next appointment gets delayed or rescheduled.
